performers: Mary Garden, soprano; Claude Debussy, piano
intro: Mélisande sings at her tower window while combing her loosened hair. Mary Garden, the first Mélisande, records the song with Debussy at the piano; after his quiet prelude, her voice is left almost entirely alone.

sections.label: A · The tower window
sections.mNote: A quiet piano prelude leads to unaccompanied singing

sections.label: B · Saints and a Sunday birth
sections.mNote: The voice names three saints, then recalls a Sunday at noon

cues.title: At the tower window
cues.text: A quiet piano prelude repeats its quavers beneath held notes. Mélisande appears at a window, combing her loosened hair. When she sings, the piano falls silent: her hair reaches down to the foot of the tower, and her tune moves freely through repeated notes.
cues.evidence: Debussy, Pelléas et Mélisande, Fromont vocal score (1902), plate E. 1416 F., Act III, scene 1, pp. 102–103: Doux et calme prelude, stage direction and unaccompanied Modéré et librement song. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d6/IMSLP33280-PMLP09094-Debussy-L088vsFR.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first Mélisande
cues.text: Mary Garden creates Mélisande at the Opéra-Comique in 1902, with André Messager conducting. Two years later she records this scene in Paris with the composer. The voice from the first production survives beside the hands that wrote its music.
cues.evidence: The Fromont vocal score’s original cast lists Mlle Garden as Mélisande and André Messager as conductor. The Record Collector’s IRCC discography, entry 106, identifies Garden and Debussy, Paris 1904. https://www.therecordcollector.org/articles/HRSandIRCCdiscographies/internationalrecordcollectorsclub.php

cues.title: Saints at the window
cues.text: After a brief piano link, Mélisande sings alone again. She names Daniel, Michael and Raphael, then says she was born on a Sunday at noon. The line slows on those last words. The piano answers quietly, taking over where her little song ends.
cues.evidence: Fromont vocal score, pp. 103–104: two-bar piano link, unaccompanied Saint Daniel et Saint Michel stanza, Sunday-birth lines, En retenant and instrumental continuation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A piano link between two stanzas
transitions.to: B · Saints and a Sunday birth
transitions.how: The piano enters beneath Mélisande’s held final word, jour. Its low quavers move under sustained treble notes through two bars of 6/4, ending at a fermata. The voice then resumes alone in 4/4, naming the saints.
transitions.evidence: Fromont vocal score, p. 103: piano entry overlapping jour, two-bar 6/4 interlude with fermata, and unaccompanied 4/4 second stanza.

source.title: Debussy, Pelléas et Mélisande · Fromont1902 vocal score, plateE.1416F.
source.locator: Act III, scene 1, printed pp. 102–104: piano prelude, two unaccompanied stanzas, a short piano link and the closing instrumental phrase.

timeline.note: Quiet piano quavers move beneath held treble notes.
Mélisande sings alone at the tower window.
The piano enters beneath the last held word, then continues alone.
The unaccompanied voice names the saints and recalls a Sunday birth.
The piano answers the voice with a quiet closing phrase.

composer.epithet: He trusted his ear over the rules — “pleasure is the law” — and made the piano, the flute and the orchestra sound new.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and went to prison for it, and there he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

His teachers could not make him out. Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, found “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament” in January 1874; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Years later, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud around 1890, he put his position plainly: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
